teaser.text: Shell plc is an integrated energy company that produces oil and gas, turns them into useful products and delivers energy to customers. Its business stretches from wells and refineries to petrol stations, factories, power companies and ships.

stock.title: Shell stock forecast
stock.meta_description: Shell's forecast weighs bear, base and bull scenarios against cash generation, ARC execution and today's valuation.
stock.opening: Shell's weighted scenario reaches 5,520.93 GBp by October 2029. It hinges on smooth ARC execution.
stock.closing: The full Shell memo also explains Shell's business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: Where could Shell's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The forecast is wide. The October 2029 bear case is 2,684.49 GBp, a -21% total return. The bull case is 8,988.18 GBp, a +148% total return. The weighted outcome is 5,520.93 GBp.

The bear case requires weaker oil and gas prices, expanding LNG supply, fading refining margins and costly ARC integration. EBITDA falls, cash conversion weakens and net debt rises, so buybacks slow and investors apply a lower multiple. The price reaches 3,211.01 GBp in October 2027 and 2,684.49 GBp in October 2029. Its 25% probability reflects Shell's demonstrated commodity exposure, although ARC production and flexible buybacks limit the likelihood of the full debt build.

The bull case requires smooth ARC execution, strong LNG demand, healthy refining margins and disciplined spending. Higher EBITDA reduces debt while stronger cash flow supports large buybacks and a higher multiple. The price reaches 6,355.43 GBp in 2027 and 8,988.18 GBp in 2029. Its 20% probability reflects the number of conditions that must succeed together, while LNG Canada Phase 2 contributes no output during the forecast period.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Shell really make?

paragraphs.text: The next claims are more concrete. Capital spending maintains and develops assets; lease payments finance the use of ships, facilities and offices; interest services debt. Share awards do not require the same immediate cash as wages, but they transfer value through dilution or offsetting buybacks. Shell’s own free-cash-flow measure also includes investing movements such as disposal proceeds, so it answers a broader question than cash left after these claims.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Shell today?

paragraphs.text: At 3780.50p, one share costs £37.805. Shell’s market value is £216,604 million: the value placed on shareholders’ claim. Enterprise value, which includes debt-like obligations and subtracts cash, is £225,747 million. It estimates the value of the operating business with its financing attached. Leases matter here because Shell reported net debt of $41.8 billion including leases, versus $12.1 billion excluding them. The earnings measure must treat those lease costs consistently.

dividend.title: Shell dividend: cash coverage and history
dividend.meta_description: Shell's dividend history, cash coverage, plans and 3.1% yield against a 9.1% free cash flow yield.
dividend.opening: Shell's dividend per share has changed over the years shown, including a cut from $0.47 to $0.16 per share in 2020. Its 3.1% dividend yield compares with a 9.1% free cash flow yield, but the real test is cash after maintenance, leases and weaker commodity prices.
dividend.closing: The full memo also examines Shell's business, its rivals, its management and the risks around its strategy.

blocks.heading: How much does Shell pay per share over the years shown?

paragraphs.text: The 2020 crisis showed why through-cycle discipline matters. Shell cut its quarterly dividend from $0.47 to $0.16 per share and stopped the next buyback tranche. The decision preserved cash when prices and demand collapsed, but it also broke a dividend record many investors had treated as dependable.

blocks.heading: Is Shell's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow yield is 9.1%, while the dividend yield is 3.1%. Free cash flow includes investing cash flows, but Shell’s definition also includes acquisitions and disposals; organic free cash flow gives a cleaner view of the existing business. The dividend appears well covered today, but the real test is cash after maintenance, leases and weaker commodity prices.

paragraphs.text: Management guides to $24–26 billion of cash capital expenditure in 2026 and $20–22 billion in 2027. It targets shareholder distributions of 40–50% of operating cash flow through the cycle, alongside 4% annual dividend growth and a $3 billion buyback.

The bear dividend falls to $1.32 and then stays near $1.24, reflecting a 20% cut after the current quarterly rate. The bull reaches $1.63, $1.73 and $1.83 because stronger cash generation supports increases above policy. The 2020 cut shows why the downside remains possible.
